critique: This first step is a generic file listing that only confirms the repo layout (tests directory under /testbed). It is weak but reasonable initial exploration, not redundant and not risky.
The grep finds where ThreadedWSGIServer is defined (basehttp.py) and where it is used (testcases.py), which are the key files for the fix. This is useful, non-repetitive exploration.
Reading basehttp.py, where ThreadedWSGIServer is defined, is a sensible exploration step. It shows how the threaded server is built and gives context for adding connection cleanup per thread.

The grep finds where LiveServerThread is defined in testcases.py (line 1476) and where it is used as server_thread_class (line 1544), so the agent knows where to read next. It is a new, read-only search with no side effects.

Reading LiveServerThread and the LiveServerTestCase setup and teardown code is useful exploration that turns up the server_class and the cleanup logic in run(). This code had not been read before, and the step is a read-only sed.

The grep for request_finished is a sensible exploration step: it shows how the signal is wired and where connection-closing receivers might hook in. That information bears directly on why per-request threads leave DB connections open.

The grep confirms that close_old_connections is wired to request_started and request_finished in django/db/__init__.py. That shows how per-request connection cleanup works, which helps explain why connections in ThreadedWSGIServer threads may not be closed (overridden connections, etc.).

Reading close_old_connections showed that it only calls close_if_unusable_or_obsolete, which does not close healthy connections. This explains why per-request threads leave connections open and is useful, non-repeated exploration.

The agent worked out that close_old_connections only closes unusable or obsolete connections, which explains why per-request threads leave connections open. It then grepped test/client.py to see how the test client handles that signal. This is reasonable investigation that adds context, though it does not point directly to the fix.

The agent read the CPython ThreadingMixIn source. It learned that process_request_thread is the per-request hook where connections could be closed, and how block_on_close and _threads affect joining at shutdown, which bears directly on the fix.
Step 10 prints the source of ThreadingMixIn.server_close, but step 9 already printed the whole ThreadingMixIn class, server_close included. The output is identical, so the step added nothing new.

The step reads socketserver._Threads and confirms that daemon threads are never added to the join list. Since Django's ThreadedWSGIServer sets daemon_threads=True, server_close() won't wait for request threads, which is a new and relevant fact for the fix.

Searching for existing tests that reference ThreadedWSGIServer is reasonable exploration, and the empty result tells the agent there is no existing coverage to reuse. The search is new, read-only, and harmless.

Locating the existing LiveServerThread test files (tests/servers/test_liveserverthread.py) is reasonable exploration and turned up files the agent can use to verify a fix. The step is new information, not a repeat, and has no side effects.

Reading the existing LiveServerThread test file is useful exploration. It shows the server_class hook and the existing connection-closing test pattern, which the agent can use to shape the fix and a regression test.

The grep for "22414" found nothing, but it was cheap, read-only exploration and it showed the codebase holds no direct reference to the earlier fix. The agent already knows the root cause (daemon threads not joined), so this step adds little, though it repeats no earlier work.

The agent grepped for the error message text and got no matches. That confirms the message is not hardcoded in the codebase, but this tangential search adds almost nothing, since the root cause (daemon threads not joined, connections not closed) was already identified in step 12.

The grep for destroy_test_db is light exploration that only shows where the function is defined and called. It is tangential, since the agent had already found the root cause (daemon threads not joined, connections not closed per thread), but it is new and harmless information.

The step looks into close_old_connections and close_if_unusable_or_obsolete. This shows how request handling closes DB connections, which bears on a fix that closes connections per thread. It is reasonable, non-repetitive exploration that tells the agent something useful.

The step reads the full body of close_if_unusable_or_obsolete. It shows that connections are closed only on errors, autocommit mismatch, or expiry of close_at, so per-request closing depends on CONN_MAX_AGE, which is useful context for designing the fix.

The grep showed how close_at is set from CONN_MAX_AGE: with max_age 0, close_at is the connect time, so request_finished closes the connection. This is useful exploration of how connections get closed per request.

The step reads the LiveServerThread code in testcases.py, the exact place the fix will go. It shows how server_class and _create_server are set up, which is what the agent needs to plan a subclass that closes connections per thread.

The grep found where request_finished is sent: HttpResponse.close() in response.py. That is useful for working out whether connections get closed per request in threaded mode. It is reasonable exploration, but it moves slowly when the fix is about closing connections when each request thread finishes.

Viewing the import block of testcases.py shows ThreadedWSGIServer is already imported from basehttp, which the agent needs before inserting a new server subclass. This is a reasonable read-only step that moves toward the edit; it is not a repeat, since only lines 1450+ had been viewed before.

The grep looks up the exact line number of the ThreadedWSGIServer import so the agent can insert its new class there, which is a small but useful step toward the edit. Step 23's numbered listing had already shown this import at line 33, though, so the lookup mostly repeats known information.

The step re-reads lines 33-45 of testcases.py, which the agent had already seen in full via `head -200 | cat -n` in step 23. It only confirms the insertion point for the planned subclass and learns nothing new.

The agent re-greps the ThreadedWSGIServer definition even though its own thought already says daemon_threads is True there, so the check only reconfirms known, unchanged code. The hypothesis about daemon threads and block_on_close is a reasonable direction, but the command adds no new information and does not move toward a fix.

The step settles on a fix approach, a non-daemon server class used through LiveServerThread.server_class, and finds the line to edit (1479). This is useful targeting for the edit and does not repeat earlier work.

The agent views the LiveServerThread definition around the server_class line before editing it, which is reasonable exploration. Part of this region may have been seen earlier, but the agent needs the exact current context to make the edit.
The step views the lines just before LiveServerThread to choose where to insert a custom server class. This read-only exploration is a reasonable step and supports the planned edit.

The grep finds the exact line number (1473) where the new class will be inserted, which helps with the upcoming sed insertion. It is a small step, and the content was already visible in step 29, where 1473 could be worked out from the 1460-1476 range.
Step 31 re-prints lines 1473-1480, which were already shown in steps 28 and 29 (lines 1460-1476 and 1475-1495). The file has not changed since then, so the step reveals nothing new.
Copying testcases.py to a .backup file is a harmless prep step so a diff can be computed later. It makes no change to the code and only slightly advances the edit.

The step writes a script that adds a ThreadedWSGIServer subclass, which closes connections after each request thread, and points LiveServerThread at it. This advances the fix, though the script has not been run yet.

Running the prepared script applies the core fix: it adds a ThreadedWSGIServer subclass that closes DB connections after each request thread, and points LiveServerThread at it. It exited 0 with no output, so the edit is not yet confirmed but is a substantive step forward.

The agent checked its scripted edit by viewing the modified region. It confirmed the new class was inserted and server_class was updated, though it also exposed formatting issues: three blank lines before the class and only one after it.
The agent tried to check its edit by running pytest, but pytest is not installed, so no test ran. It did learn that it needs Django's own runtests.py instead.

The step lists the top-level .py files in /testbed to find a test runner, and the output shows runtests.py is not at the root. That is small but useful exploration toward finding how to run the tests (it lives in tests/runtests.py).
The step found tests/runtests.py, which the agent needs because pytest isn't installed. This is a quick, read-only exploration step that moves verification forward.

Running the servers.test_liveserverthread suite with runtests.py is a reasonable check of the patched LiveServerThread, but it failed because django isn't importable. That failure is still useful: the agent now knows it must set PYTHONPATH or install Django before tests can run.

The step did an editable install of Django so the test suite can run, which is a reasonable setup step that moves the work toward verification. It installs packages into the environment but goes no further than that, so it is not destructive.

With Django installed, the agent ran the liveserverthread tests against its edit: 2 tests, 1 skipped, OK. That is useful verification that nothing broke, though it does not exercise the race condition itself.
Running git status is a quick, harmless check. It confirms the repo state and that only django/test/testcases.py is modified, which is useful before producing the diff patch.

Staging the modified file is a small step toward producing the patch. It is not destructive and goes nowhere outside the task, but it adds little because git diff of the working tree would have worked without it.
The step writes the staged diff of django/test/testcases.py to patch.txt, which is the required way to produce the submission. It is not repeated work and it touches nothing except a new patch file.

Reading patch.txt is a reasonable check that the generated diff contains the intended change: a ThreadedWSGIServer subclass that closes connections after each request thread. It confirms the work so far, though the patch has a stray extra blank line and close_all may close the overridden shared connection in the in-memory sqlite case.

The agent ran the full servers test suite, a broader regression check than the earlier single-module run. All 25 tests passed with 1 skipped, which confirms the new server class doesn't break existing live server behavior.

Running staticfiles_tests.test_liveserver is a reasonable extra regression check on another LiveServerTestCase suite that hasn't been run yet, and it passed. It is a read-only test run with no side effects.
The agent tried to run a test label 'testcases' that doesn't exist in the test suite, so the step ended in a ModuleNotFoundError and verified nothing. It did not repeat earlier work and was harmless.
Step 49 re-prints the staged diff, which step 45 already showed via patch.txt. The output is identical, so nothing new was learned and the task did not advance.

The step submits a patch that was exercised by the passing `servers` and staticfiles live-server tests, so the completion is not unverified. The patch still fails the hidden tests, likely because calling `connections.close_all()` in every request thread doesn't match the expected fix. The run looked sound but still failed.
The agent made no valid tool call, so it got only a format error and learned nothing about the PostgreSQL client env bug. This first step was wasted but did no harm.

Listing the directory is reasonable initial orientation: it confirms the repo root and shows the django/ and tests/ layout. It is not redundant, since step 0 was a tool-call error, and it is a harmless read-only command.
The step produced no tool call and only triggered a format error, so it added nothing. It repeats the same no-tool-call failure from step 0.
The step produced no tool call and only triggered the same error already seen in steps 0 and 2, so nothing advanced. It repeats an earlier failed non-action and learns nothing new.

The find command is a sensible first look for client files, but head -30 cut the list off before the postgresql client.py appeared. It still showed that the backends keep their client code in django/db/backends/*/client.py, which points to where the fix belongs.

The step lists every backend client.py and finds django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py and base/client.py, which are the files the fix needs. It is a quick, read-only search that narrows the earlier truncated results.
Reading the postgresql client file shows the bug's source directly: `env = {}` is always returned, even when no options are set. This is useful, non-redundant, read-only exploration.

Reading base/client.py is useful exploration. It shows that runshell merges os.environ only when env is truthy, so an empty dict reaches subprocess.run as an empty environment, which confirms the bug mechanism.

The step checks that the referenced commit is in the git history, which is reasonable groundwork for reading its diff to understand how the bug was introduced. The thought briefly gets confused about whether an empty dict is truthy, but the command is harmless and gives useful context.
The step has no tool call and an empty thought, so it returned only an error message. It did no exploration, made no edit, and gave the agent nothing new to use.

Running git show --stat on the referenced commit is reasonable read-only investigation, and it shows which files were touched by the change that introduced the bug. It adds context, though the bug mechanism (empty dict being falsy) was already visible from the earlier reads.

Viewing the commit diff for the postgresql client shows that it used to copy os.environ and now returns a bare `env = {}`, which confirms where the bug came from. This is useful, read-only investigation that does not repeat earlier steps.

Reading the mysql client confirms that other backends return env=None when no variables are needed, while postgresql returns {}. This comparison narrows down where the fix should go and is new, harmless information.

Reading the sqlite3 client is a reasonable read-only check that other backends return None for env. It confirms the bug is limited to postgresql's empty-dict return, which narrows where the fix should go.

Reading the Oracle client is reasonable exploration and new information: it confirms that Oracle returns None for env, so the bug is isolated to PostgreSQL's empty dict. It is read-only and non-repetitive, though it was not strictly necessary.

The grep confirms that postgresql is the only backend that initializes env to an empty dict. That finishes the survey of backends and supports a fix in the base client. It is a cheap, useful check and not a repeat of the earlier per-file reads.

The grep finds no other backend that returns a literal empty dict as env, which confirms the bug is confined to postgresql. It is a cheap, reasonable check that differs from the earlier `env = {}` search.

Reading the spatialite client is reasonable exploration. It confirms the client inherits from sqlite3, which returns None for env, so it is unaffected. The agent had not opened this file before, though it is marginal.

The agent weighed two fix options and then ran a find command that located the existing client test files, which helps it build a reproduction or test next. This is useful exploration and has no side effects.
The agent reads the base client test file to see how tests are structured before writing a repro. This is reasonable read-only exploration, though the file has only a NotImplementedError test.

Grepping for __version__ only returned `get_version(VERSION)`, which gives no actual version number and nothing useful for fixing the empty-env bug. It is a harmless read-only command, and no earlier step had run it.

The agent wrote a repro script, but it failed at import with ModuleNotFoundError for asgiref, so it confirmed nothing about the env bug. The only new fact is that the environment lacks dependencies, which is of some use for later steps.

Installing the missing asgiref and sqlparse dependencies directly fixes the ModuleNotFoundError that blocked the repro script, so the agent can continue. It repeats no earlier work, and adding packages to the test environment is a minor, task-relevant change that is not destructive.

Once the dependencies were installed, rerunning the repro script confirmed the bug: the postgresql client returns an empty dict for env, so runshell would hand an empty environment to the subprocess. This is useful confirmation, and it does not just repeat the earlier run, which failed on a missing import.

Viewing base/client.py with line numbers, just before editing it, pinpointed the faulty `if env:` check at lines 24-26 that the fix will target. It is a harmless read-only command, and it may repeat an earlier view whose steps are not shown here.

The step only backs up the base client file before editing. That is a harmless preparatory action, and the thought confirms the chosen fix (`if env is not None`), so it moves the task forward a little.

The step applies the core fix, changing `if env:` to `if env is not None:` in the base client, so an empty dict env is now merged with os.environ. The edit is targeted and a backup was made first, though the change has not been verified yet.

Viewing the file after the sed edit confirms that line 24 now reads `if env is not None:`, so the edit landed. This is a legitimate post-edit check, not a repeat of earlier work, since the file had changed.

The grep looked for other backends that return env, which is a reasonable check of how the fix in the base class affects the other clients. It is read-only and new, though it is not a test of the edit.
The grep was overly broad and its output was noisy, but it did confirm that oracle's client returns `args, None`. That fits the `is not None` fix and moves the backend survey forward a little.

The cat command partly failed on the bogus '40-60' argument, but it still printed the full postgresql client. That confirms `env = {}` is returned unconditionally, which is the root cause the agent was checking.
The agent finds the postgresql dbshell test file, which is a reasonable exploratory step toward running the existing tests. It is new information, not a repeat of earlier work.

Reading the postgresql dbshell test file is sensible exploration. It shows that test_nopass expects an empty dict ({}) for env, which bears on whether the fix belongs in the postgres client or in the base runshell merge logic.

The agent tried to run the existing postgresql dbshell tests to check its base client change, but pytest is not installed, so nothing ran. It did learn that pytest isn't available, so it needs a different runner such as tests/runtests.py.

The agent tried running the dbshell tests through `python -m django test` with global settings, and it failed with a missing pytz import. That is still useful, since it shows this environment needs a different test runner (e.g., tests/runtests.py) or dependency setup.
The step installs pytz, the missing dependency that made the previous test run fail, so the test suite can now run. It is a small, needed environment fix with no destructive effect on the repository.

Writing a minimal settings file is a reasonable setup step toward running the dbshell tests through the Django runner, since earlier attempts failed for lack of pytest and pytz. It creates a stray file in the repo root, but that is minor and not destructive.

The test run failed with ModuleNotFoundError because the agent ran from /testbed rather than tests/ or via runtests.py, but the failure shows that the module path has to be adjusted. That is a usable signal for the next attempt.
The agent fixed the import path and ran the postgresql dbshell tests. All 10 ran OK with 1 skipped, which shows the base client change doesn't break the existing tests.

The step adds a mock-based repro script showing that the PostgreSQL client still returns an empty env dict, yet runshell now passes os.environ to subprocess.run. This directly verifies the base-client fix beyond what the existing tests covered. The script is a new file in /testbed and leaves existing tests untouched.

The step checks a new case: a PostgreSQL password, where the env dict is non-empty and gets merged with os.environ. The output confirms that PGPASSWORD and PATH both reach subprocess.run, which complements the empty-dict check from step 39.

A quick grep shows the mysql client only ever sets env to None or a non-empty dict, so the empty-dict case is ruled out for that backend. It is a cheap, read-only check of another backend affected by the base client fix.

The agent tried to run the whole tests.dbshell package. Test discovery crashed with a TypeError because tests/ is a namespace package, so no tests ran, but the agent learned it must target the test modules individually or use runtests.py.

Running git diff to confirm that only base/client.py was changed is a sensible pre-submission check and moves toward producing the patch. The agent misread the step-42 failure as missing client libraries, but that misdiagnosis does not undermine this harmless read-only step.

Viewing the git diff confirms the single change (`if env:` → `if env is not None:`), which is reasonable pre-submission verification. It's read-only and not a duplicate of earlier output, since only the file names had been listed before.

The script checked env handling for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite after the fix, and the MySQL/SQLite None behavior is new information. It crashed on the Oracle client import (no cx_Oracle), so the password cases never ran, and the PostgreSQL no-password case mostly repeats the step-40 check.

The agent's reasoning was muddled: it wrongly said an empty dict is truthy. The script it ran corrected this by showing that under the original logic `{}` is falsy and goes to subprocess as an empty env, while the fix merges os.environ, so the step clarified and confirmed the fix's mechanism.

The thought correctly works out from step 46's output that an empty dict is falsy, which confirms the `is not None` fix. The command itself only greps base/client.py again, content already shown in the step 44 diff, as a lead-in to an optional docstring edit.

Running the base client test suite after the fix is a reasonable regression check, and it passed. The agent had already said in step 43 that unit tests were run, so this may partly repeat that check, but it targets the edited module directly and is cheap.

Running the MySQL dbshell tests after the base client fix is a fair regression check, and all 9 tests passed. These tests mostly exercise settings_to_cmd_args_env rather than runshell, but they still confirm nothing broke.

The agent ran the sqlite dbshell tests and all 2 passed, which is a reasonable regression check after changing base/client.py from `if env:` to `if env is not None:`. The step is new, read-only, and does not repeat earlier test runs.
The step writes the git diff of the edited source file to patch.txt, as the instructions require. It is a needed packaging step after earlier steps verified the change with passing tests.

Running cat on patch.txt checks that the patch file contains the intended one-line change from `if env:` to `if env is not None:`. That is a sensible check of the deliverable, since step 51's git diff printed nothing to the console.

Running git status is a reasonable pre-submit check. It shows that only client.py among tracked files was modified, though several untracked scratch files exist. It is low-cost and confirms the patch scope, though the thought says 'again', so it is partly a recheck.

This step writes yet another verification script, re-checking the PostgreSQL empty-dict and MySQL cases. Earlier scripts (test_empty_dict.py, verify_fix.py, test_all_backends.py) and the backend test suites had already confirmed the one-line `if env is not None` fix, so it adds no new information.

The agent submitted a minimal base-client fix (`if env is not None`) that it had checked with existing tests and a custom script, which is a sound process. The hidden tests likely expect PostgreSQL's `settings_to_cmd_args_env` itself to return None instead of an empty dict, so the run failed despite reasonable, verified steps.
The agent produced no valid tool call, so it gathered nothing and did not advance the task. It is the first step, so it repeats nothing, and it had no side effects.
The agent again sent a response with no tool call and got the same error as step 0. Nothing moved forward and nothing new was learned.

The agent searched for files whose names contain 'spanselector' and got nothing back. SpanSelector lives in widgets.py, but the empty result still shows the agent it must search by content rather than by filename, so this is reasonable early exploration.

The broader grep located the files that define and test SpanSelector (widgets.py, test_widgets.py), which is useful exploration. It is a read-only search and does not repeat earlier work, since the previous search only matched filenames.
Listing the repo root is cheap orientation and does not repeat any earlier step, though it adds little since the relevant file was already found. It still counts as reasonable early exploration.
The agent located the SpanSelector class definition at line 1991 of widgets.py. This is a useful exploration step toward reading the relevant code.
Reading the SpanSelector class source is sensible exploration. It turned up useful details such as the Rectangle created at (0, 0) and the setup of the edge handles, both of which relate to the bug.

Reading the rest of SpanSelector turned up the root cause: _setup_edge_handle passes self.extents (initially (0,0)) to ToolLineHandles, which uses ax.axvline and so expands the axes limits to include 0. This is useful, non-repeated exploration with no side effects.

The agent wrote a reasonable reproduction script that prints the axis limits before and after creating the SpanSelector, but running it failed because matplotlib cannot be imported in this environment. The failure still tells the agent something useful: it needs a different Python interpreter or environment setup before it can reproduce the bug.

The step tried importing matplotlib from the source lib directory and found that numpy is missing too, so the current python interpreter lacks the needed dependencies. This is useful environment diagnosis that will guide the agent toward the right interpreter or environment.

Installing numpy via apt-get resolves the import error from step 9 and lets the agent move toward running its reproduction script, so it is reasonable environment setup. It is not redundant, and adding a package is non-destructive, though an unactivated testbed environment may have been the cleaner route.

Installing the local matplotlib in editable mode is a sensible, successful setup step that unblocks reproducing the bug. It is not repeated work, though pip pulled in numpy 2.4.2, which may not be compatible with this older dev matplotlib build.

The step successfully reproduced the bug: after SpanSelector is created, xlim grows from (9.5, 20.5) to (-1, 21) and now includes zero. That confirms the issue and gives a baseline to check a fix against.

Grepping widgets.py for autoscale is cheap and useful exploration. The empty result tells the agent that widgets.py makes no explicit autoscale calls, which points toward the implicit autoscaling done by axvline/axhline.

The step compares interactive=False with interactive=True and shows that only the interactive path expands the xlim. This narrows the cause to the interactive-only code, likely the handle lines placed at x=0, and is useful diagnostic progress.

This step showed that a hidden axvline at x=0 still widens the xlims to include 0. That points the bug at the handle lines that interactive mode creates, which is new and useful diagnostic information.

After step 15 confirmed that an invisible axvline at x=0 expands the limits, this step greps for the axvline definition in _axes.py to see how it changes dataLim. It is a sensible next diagnostic move: new, read-only, and it locates the code to inspect.

The step reads the axvline definition, but the 30 lines of context stop inside the docstring and never reach the implementation (autoscale/dataLim handling). It is reasonable exploration toward the root cause, yet it yielded little usable information.

Step 18 widens the read of axvline to show its body, past the docstring that step 17 already printed. The body explains why the invisible line still expands the limits, so the step adds information even though the top part repeats.

The step looks at the axvline body it just read and correctly finds that it calls _request_autoscale_view whenever x lies outside the current bounds. It then greps for line_fun and finds the exact lines in ToolLineHandles that need changing, which narrows down where the fix goes.
The step reads the ToolLineHandles constructor around the line_fun usage. This gives the exact context the agent needs to edit the axvline/axhline handle creation that triggers autoscaling.

The agent read the top of widgets.py to see what is imported. It confirmed that Line2D is already imported, which it needs for building the handle lines by hand without calling axvline. This is reasonable preparation for the planned fix and is safe and not repetitive.

The grep for "dataLim" in lines.py came back empty, which settles that Line2D has no flag to keep itself out of the data limits. That is a small but useful result for choosing a fix that avoids axvline's autoscale request.

This step re-greps the ToolLineHandles class, mostly repeating lines 2360-2400 already shown in step 20. The few new lines (set_visible, set_animated, remove, closest) do not bear on the autoscale fix.

The step confirms that get_xaxis_transform defaults to which='grid', which the agent needs to build Line2D handles manually with the same transform axvline uses. It is a small, reasonable read-only lookup that has not been done before.

The experiment shows that axvline(0) expands the xlim to include 0, and that a manually added Line2D with the xaxis transform leaves the limits alone. This confirms the planned fix approach. The manual-line check ran after an explicit set_xlim, which turns autoscale off, so it is a weaker comparison, but it still yields useful evidence and the step was a safe scratch test.

The agent re-viewed the ToolLineHandles __init__ lines just before editing them, which is a sensible check of exact line numbers before patching. Most of this content was already shown in step 23's grep output, so it is somewhat redundant, but it confirms the edit location.

This step re-reads lines 2358-2372, which step 26 had just printed unchanged as part of lines 2350-2380. Adding relative line numbers confirms the replacement range a little, but the agent learns almost nothing new.

The step uses a Python script to swap the axvline/axhline calls in ToolLineHandles.__init__ for manually created Line2D objects with axis transforms, and the script's output confirms it found and replaced the correct block. This directly applies the fix validated in step 25 and stays within the task's scope.

Importing the edited module after the in-place rewrite is a reasonable syntax sanity check, and it confirms the module still loads. It is a small but real step toward verification and does not repeat earlier work.
Running the reproduction script after the edit confirms that SpanSelector no longer expands the xlim to include 0, which verifies the fix. This step is progress and is neither redundant nor risky.
The agent tried to run the SpanSelector regression tests and found that pytest isn't installed. No tests ran, but this is useful information about the environment.

Installing pytest lets the agent run the existing widget tests after it found pytest missing, so it is reasonable progress. It upgraded pluggy as a side effect, which is a minor environment change but not destructive to the task.

The pytest run hit a collection error: pyparsing deprecation warnings are treated as errors, likely because of the pytest upgrade in the previous step, so none of the SpanSelector tests ran. The step still showed that test collection is blocked by an environment problem, which the agent can work around (e.g., with -W flags).

Adding -W ignore fixed the collection error from step 33, which is useful to know, but -k SpanSelector selected none of the 34 tests because they are named with underscores, so no test actually ran. The step is still progress: it showed that collection now works and that the filter needs changing, and it was neither a repeat nor destructive.

The grep found no class named SpanSelector, which shows the tests are not grouped in such a class and explains the deselection. It is a cheap, read-only diagnostic step that tells the agent to search for test function names instead.

The grep showed where SpanSelector is used in test_widgets.py (lines 208-273) after the class-name search came back empty. That tells the agent the tests are module-level functions rather than a class, so it can now target them.

Step 34 had already shown that `-W ignore` gets the test file collected (34 items, all deselected only because `-k SpanSelector` matched no function names). Switching to `PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore` hit the same pyparsing collection error, so the step yielded nothing usable.

The agent re-ran the full test file with `--disable-warnings`, which only hides the warning summary and cannot stop pytest.ini's warnings-as-errors filter. It got the same pyparsing collection error as step 37 and learned nothing new, instead of checking pytest.ini or passing `-W ignore::DeprecationWarning` / `-p no:warnings`.

Targeting the specific pyparsing warning category with -W got past the collection error, so tests now run. The run hit a RectangleSelector failure that is probably unrelated to the change, which is useful to learn.

The grep turned up the specific SpanSelector test function names (test_span_selector, test_span_selector_drag, test_span_selector_direction), which lets the agent run just those tests instead of the whole file. That is useful targeting after the full run hit an unrelated failure, and it is a different query from the earlier grep for class names and constructor calls.
